summary: The Linear feedback shift register calculator turns the initial state, the connection coefficients and number of digits in the output/steps into message length. Think of it as a shortcut for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Editing anything puts the results away until the next press of Calculate — change one value at a time and the updated answer tells you what that value was worth.

sections.title: How does the Linear feedback shift register calculator work?
sections.html:
The Linear feedback shift register calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports message length in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the LFSR type, the type of output and the dangerous calculations); then you type in the initial state (seed), the connection coefficients and number of digits in the output/steps.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Linear feedback shift register calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Message length=((initial state (seed)))
Coefficients length=((connection coefficients))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Initial state (seed) = 10, Connection coefficients = 10, LFSR type set to Fibonacci and Type of output set to Output. The calculator returns Coefficients length = 2 and Message length = 2.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Coefficients length = 2 and Message length = 2 should be roughly the size you expected from Initial state (seed) = 10 and Connection coefficients = 10.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Linear feedback shift register calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the initial state, the connection coefficients and number of digits in the output/steps — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Linear feedback shift register calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns message length, derived from the initial state, the connection coefficients and number of digits in the output/steps. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Linear feedback shift register calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial state, the connection coefficients and number of digits in the output/steps, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (15 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Coefficients length = 2. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Linear feedback shift register calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
